ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Pulmonology (asthma) Consultation — Mary McLeod Bethune — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Diagnosis visit: spirometry, FeNO and echocardiogram results with the pulmonology consultation; asthma confirmed, heart failure excluded, hypertensive heart disease found; start of budesonide-formoterol as maintenance and reliever

text.paragraph: Four months of wheeze, night cough and breathlessness on stairs in a 72-year-old never-smoking woman who has been told for many years that she has asthma but has never had lung function testing and has been treated with albuterol alone. Please confirm or refute asthma with spirometry before and after bronchodilator, DLCO and FeNO, help separate it from COPD and heart disease, and advise on treatment. [S]

list.item: Does she have asthma, COPD, or both, and does heart disease contribute to her breathlessness?
How should the lung function results be interpreted, given the move to race-neutral reference equations?
What treatment do you recommend now, and how should albuterol-only treatment be replaced?
What is her inflammatory phenotype, and is she, or could she become, a candidate for biologic therapy?
Which comorbidities are worsening her asthma, and how should they be managed?
What monitoring, action plan and vaccinations should primary care provide?

text.paragraph: Mrs. Bethune, 72, is seen at the request of Dr. Harrington-Mbeki for four months of worsening wheeze, night cough and breathlessness on exertion, on a background of asthma diagnosed clinically many years ago and never confirmed. She uses albuterol most days and has never had an inhaled corticosteroid. Triggers are colds, dust, perfume and humid air. She has never smoked. She has nasal blockage, postnasal drip and reduced smell, and evening heartburn. She has had no oral corticosteroid course, emergency visit or admission for asthma in the past year. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Mary Jane McLeod was born on July 10, 1875, near Mayesville, South Carolina, the fifteenth of seventeen children of Samuel and Patsy McLeod. Her parents, and eight of her older siblings, had been enslaved; after emancipation the family bought five acres of land and farmed cotton. [D]

She was the only McLeod child to get an education, first at a Presbyterian mission school near Mayesville and then at Scotia Seminary. In 1898 she married Albertus Bethune; they separated after about nine years without divorcing, and he died in 1918. [D]

In 1904 she founded a school for Black girls in Daytona Beach, Florida. She opened McLeod Hospital there in 1911, which the National Park Service says played a critical role in containing the influenza pandemic of 1918, and she and her students faced down the Ku Klux Klan at the school. The school merged with the Cookman Institute (dated 1923 by the National Park Service; named Bethune-Cookman College in 1929 according to another reference), and she was its president until 1942. [D]

She was president of the National Association of Colored Women from 1924, received the NAACP's Spingarn Medal in 1935, and founded the National Council of Negro Women on December 5, 1935. She directed the Division of Negro Affairs of the National Youth Administration from the mid-1930s until it closed in 1943 and led the informal group of Black federal advisers known as the Black Cabinet. She said of her place in Washington: "When they see me, they know that the Negro is present." [D]

For many years she suffered from chronic asthma, which increasingly restricted her ability to travel, and after a particularly severe attack in 1942 she gave up the presidency of Bethune-Cookman College. [D]

The guide to her foundation's papers lists "Bethune asthma attacks" as a major topic of her administrative correspondence in the first half of 1943, and describes her health problems as a recurrent subject of her correspondence in those years. [D]

From 1935 she lived in a series of apartments in Washington, D.C., while keeping her home, known as the Retreat, on the campus in Daytona Beach. In December 1943 she and the National Council of Negro Women bought 1318 Vermont Avenue, which became the council's first national headquarters and her Washington residence. [D]

tr.td: Wheeze, cough and breathlessness for four months: waking with cough and tight chest two or three nights a week, breathless on one flight of stairs, relieved by albuterol, worse with colds, dust and strong scents; known asthma for many years but never confirmed by lung function testing and never treated with an inhaled steroid. Asthma, COPD and heart failure to be distinguished: spirometry with bronchodilator response, FeNO and an echocardiogram booked
S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to her documented chronic asthma. Superseded by the diagnosis at the second visit.
Blocked nose, thick postnasal drip and a reduced sense of smell for years, worse in the last year; no nosebleeds; never seen by an ear, nose and throat specialist
S — Synthetic upper-airway symptoms; superseded by the diagnosis of chronic rhinosinusitis after nasal endoscopy.
Gastro-esophageal reflux: heartburn and an acid taste two or three evenings a week, worse after late meals and lying down; no trouble swallowing, vomiting, black stools or weight loss
S — Synthetic comorbidity of asthma; not a claim about her real health.
Obesity, class 1 (BMI 33.1); she wants to walk more and to keep up with her work, and agreed to talk about it
S — Synthetic comorbidity recorded in her words and with her agreement; not a claim about her real weight.

Asthma, confirmed: variable airflow obstruction (FEV1 64 percent predicted, rising 270 mL or 21 percent after bronchodilator, with a normal post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC of 0.72 and normal DLCO); type 2 inflammation (FeNO 46 ppb, blood eosinophils 0.42 x10^3/uL, total IgE 210, house dust mite sensitization); not COPD and not heart failure. Uncontrolled at diagnosis on albuterol alone
S — Synthetic modern confirmation linked to her documented chronic asthma.

Hypertensive heart disease without heart failure: clinic blood pressure 152/88 and 146/86, home average 144/84; mild concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with grade 1 diastolic dysfunction and a normal ejection fraction (62 percent); BNP 48 pg/mL

list.item: Asthma, confirmed, uncontrolled, with type 2 inflammation (J45.40). Question 1: this is asthma. The 270 mL, 21 percent bronchodilator response confirms variable airflow obstruction, and the post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC of 0.72 with a normal DLCO argues against COPD, which in any case would be unusual in a never smoker. Question 2: read with race-neutral GLI Global equations, as the American Thoracic Society now recommends, her FEV1 is 64 percent of predicted; race-based equations would have set a lower predicted value for her and made the impairment look milder, which is one way asthma in Black patients has been under-recognized. Question 4: FeNO 46 ppb, eosinophils 0.42, total IgE 210 and dust mite sensitization show type 2 (allergic and eosinophilic) inflammation. She does not have severe asthma, because she has never been treated with an inhaled corticosteroid, so biologic therapy is not indicated now; if she remained uncontrolled on optimized step 4 to 5 treatment, or had repeated oral corticosteroid courses, she would qualify for assessment, and anti-IL-5 or anti-IL-4 receptor therapy would fit her phenotype. [S]

Hypertensive heart disease without heart failure (I11.9). Question 1, continued: her breathlessness is not cardiac. BNP is 48, the ejection fraction is normal, the left atrium is not enlarged and there is no pulmonary hypertension. The LVH and grade 1 diastolic dysfunction reflect untreated hypertension, which should be treated; a beta-blocker should be avoided. [S]

Chronic nasal symptoms (R09.81). Question 5: probable chronic rhinosinusitis, which worsens asthma control; nasal endoscopy will confirm it and look for polyps, which would also matter for any later biologic choice. Reflux should be treated for its own symptoms; obesity can add to breathlessness, but here asthma is the main cause. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Harrington-Mbeki's intake note and results: chest X-ray with mild hyperinflation and normal heart size; ECG with LVH by voltage; blood eosinophils 0.42; BNP 48; Asthma Control Test 13. This morning, in our laboratory, with GLI Global race-neutral equations: FEV1 1.30 L (64 percent predicted) before and 1.57 L after albuterol 400 mcg (+270 mL, +21 percent); FEV1/FVC 0.64 before and 0.72 after; DLCO 17.2 (92 percent predicted); FeNO 46 ppb. Total IgE 210 IU/mL; specific IgE positive to house dust mite, negative to cat, dog, cockroach and mold. Transthoracic echocardiogram this morning: ejection fraction 62 percent, mild concentric LVH, grade 1 diastolic dysfunction, normal left atrium and right ventricle, estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure 28 mmHg. [S]

list.item: Question 3: stop albuterol alone and start GINA track 1 budesonide-formoterol 160/4.5 mcg as maintenance and reliever: one inhalation twice daily and one as needed, up to 12 a day (step 3). [S]
Check inhaler technique and adherence at every visit and correct them before any step-up; add a spacer if the technique with the pressurized inhaler is poor. [S]

Question 6: a written asthma action plan with peak flow zones, a peak flow meter and a diary to set her personal best; review six weeks after starting and within a week of any exacerbation; Asthma Control Test at each visit; repeat spirometry and FeNO after three to six months. [S]
Treat the upper airway: intranasal fluticasone and saline now, and ear, nose and throat review with nasal endoscopy. [S]
Treat symptomatic reflux with an eight-week course of a proton pump inhibitor and meal timing; it is not a treatment for asthma. [S]
Hypertension: amlodipine or another agent without beta-blockade; avoid nonselective beta-blockers, including eye drops. [S]
Biologic therapy is not indicated now; repeat blood eosinophils and reassess if asthma is uncontrolled on step 4 to 5 treatment or she needs two or more oral corticosteroid courses in a year. [S]
Vaccines: pneumococcal vaccine now; influenza, COVID-19 and RSV in the autumn; house dust mite covers for the bedding. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Harrington-Mbeki the same day. The results were explained to Mrs. Bethune in plain words, including why the reference equations matter and why her breathlessness is asthma rather than her heart or her weight. She asked for a copy of her results and decides who else receives this note. [S]

Follow-up: Pulmonology review after the repeat spirometry in three to six months, or sooner if an exacerbation occurs or control is not achieved; Dr. Harrington-Mbeki continues primary care and shares the monitoring. [S]
